topic: installing and running a wood-fired hot tub in a garden

provenance.author: glowny-en-b
provenance.notes: 10 turns, user first; variant a is fill, firewood and schedule arithmetic with closed task questions, base is an exploratory dialogue about siting, first fire and water care. Grounded external referent: the stove, introduced in turn 0 (sits inside the tub behind slats, burns logs) and mentioned in the sentence directly before every insertion (burns logs, upper port, low ports, ticking, drawing hard).

a: Here is the tub delivery, and the water volume needs working out before the first fill.
The tub is round at one point eight metres across inside and one metre deep.
The fill line sits at eighty centimetres, and the maker gives the volume as two thousand litres.
The hose delivers twelve litres a minute at the garden tap, measured with a bucket.
How many minutes does the fill take at that steady rate from empty?
base: The hot tub arrived on a pallet, and the yard has a level gravel pad waiting for it.
It is the wooden kind with a stove that sits inside the tub behind a fence of slats.
The stove burns logs, and the whole thing works with no pump and no wires at all.
The seller waved away most of our questions with the word simple.
What order should the first afternoon run so nothing gets done twice?

a: Two thousand litres at twelve litres a minute takes one hundred sixty-seven minutes, rounding up.
That is two hours and forty-seven minutes of steady running from the garden tap.
Starting the hose at one in the afternoon puts the fill done just before four.
A second hose at the same rate would halve the figure to eighty-four minutes, rounded up.
Is a second hose worth borrowing for the first fill this weekend?
base: Level the pad first with a long spirit level, because two thousand litres punishes any slope.
Roll the tub in, set it on its bearers, and check the level again across two directions.
The stove must never burn dry, so water goes in before any match is struck.
Fill past the upper stove port before lighting, and the metal stays safe for years.
Does the pad drain freely, or does rain stand on the gravel after a storm?

a: Now work out the wood, because the maker quotes one heating from a single barrow of logs.
A barrow holds fifteen logs, and the store presently holds ninety logs in total.
Each soak takes one heating, and we plan two soaks a week through the autumn.
Count the barrows in the store first and then the weeks they cover.
How many full weeks of two soaks each does the store of ninety support?
base: The pad drains well, and the bearers came with the kit cut to length already.
The stove ports are low on the wall, and the paperwork repeats the warning about dry burning twice.
The tub is rolled in, sitting level both ways on the first try.
The chimney sections stack to about two metres and end in a little rain cap.
How full should the tub be before the very first fire is lit?

a: Ninety logs at fifteen to the barrow makes six barrows standing in the store.
Six barrows support six heatings, which is three weeks at two soaks a week.
Autumn runs about twelve weeks here, so the store covers a quarter of the season.
Covering the rest calls for eighteen more barrows, or two hundred seventy logs.
Does the wood man sell by the load, and how many logs does a load hold?
base: Fill until the water stands a hand above the upper port, then the first fire is safe.
The first burn should be gentle, one layer of logs, to let the stove seal and settle.
The stove will tick and smell of paint for an hour, and that is fine.
Stir the tub now and then with the paddle, because the heat rises in layers.
Have you got a floating thermometer, or are you trusting your elbows on this?

a: One correction from the shed: the barrow holds eighteen logs, not fifteen as first counted.
Rework the barrow count for the store and the weeks it covers.
Keep the plan at two soaks a week right through the autumn.
Then give the extra logs needed to reach twelve weeks in full.
How many barrows does the store hold at eighteen logs to the barrow?
base: There is a floating thermometer in the box, shaped like a small yellow duck.
The first fire is burning now, one gentle layer, and the paint smell is fading.
The duck already reads twenty-one degrees after the first hour of gentle burning.
The stove draws hard once the chimney warms, better than the fireplace indoors ever has.
How long should the climb to thirty-eight degrees take from a cold start?

a: At eighteen logs each, the store of ninety makes five level barrows exactly.
Five heatings give two full weeks of two soaks, with one heating left over.
Check the leftover heating as well, because it carries into the first week.
Twelve weeks at two soaks calls for twenty-four heatings from first to last.
That is twenty-four barrows, or four hundred thirty-two logs at the new count.
After the ninety in the store, does the order come to three hundred forty-two logs?
base: From a cold start in autumn, expect two to three hours to reach thirty-eight degrees.
The climb is slow at first and quick at the end, once the whole mass is moving.
Feed the stove little and often rather than stacking the box full at the start.
Close the air down when the duck shows thirty-six, and the last two degrees arrive on their own.
Who has earned the first soak after all this hauling and stacking of logs?

a: Now lay out the soak evening as five steps with times for the notebook.
Write the five step names down the page with a time beside each.
Lighting takes fifteen minutes, heating takes one hundred fifty, and checking takes fifteen.
The soak itself runs sixty minutes and the close down takes thirty.
The whole evening starts with the lighting step at four o'clock sharp.
Which clock time does the soak begin if every step runs to plan?
base: The first soak went to the one who stacked the logs, and it was worth every barrow.
The water sat at thirty-eight for a good hour with only a log or two added.
Now we are wondering about the water itself, because it looked cloudy this morning.
Nothing has been added to it, no salts and no bottles of anything.
How long can one fill of plain water be kept sweet between soaks?

a: Lighting runs from four until quarter past, and heating follows straight after it.
Heating runs from quarter past four until quarter to seven on the page.
Checking takes quarter to seven until seven, and the soak begins at seven exactly.
The soak ends at eight and the close down finishes the evening at half past.
Does the half past eight finish match the notebook line you wrote earlier?
base: Plain water in a wooden tub stays sweet for three or four soaks at most.
Cloudy on day two usually means it went in warm and stood covered too long.
Drain, rinse the boards, and refill rather than chasing one fill with chemicals.
The garden will happily drink two thousand litres if you drain toward the beds.
Is there a fall from the tub valve toward those beds, even a slight one?

a: Print the drain down as four jobs in order for Sunday morning.
Job one is the valve, job two is the rinse, job three is the wipe, job four is the cover.
The valve empties the tub in ninety minutes and each other job takes twenty.
Work starts at nine and the jobs run one after another with no gaps.
Which clock time is the cover job done under that Sunday running order?
base: There is a gentle fall from the valve to the flower beds, maybe half a metre.
A length of the old blue pipe reaches the beds with a metre to spare.
We will drain every fourth soak and give the boards a rinse while it empties.
The cover keeps the leaves out, and the duck lives on the shelf between times.
Is there anything about frost we should fear once the real winter arrives?

a: The valve runs from nine until half past ten on the Sunday order.
The rinse takes half past ten until ten to eleven, and the wipe follows.
The wipe ends at ten past eleven and the cover job starts straight away.
The cover is done at half past eleven, closing the morning in two and a half hours.
Every job now carries its clock time on the printed Sunday list.
The afternoon stays free after that, with nothing left on the Sunday page.
base: Frost is the one enemy, because still water and iron fittings both suffer in a hard freeze.
Either soak twice a week and keep the mass warm, or drain fully before a cold snap.
Never leave it half full in January, because ice grips hardest at a part filled wall.
Prop the cover a little through winter so air moves and the boards stay sound.
Do that much, and the tub will be ready the first mild evening of spring.
